strengths: Addresses a practical and relevant problem: reducing training data for motion forecasting while paying attention to underrepresented dense-traffic scenarios, which is meaningful for autonomous driving datasets.
The paper gives a clear high-level motivation for difficulty-aware coreset construction and evaluates on Argoverse with standard trajectory metrics including minADE, minFDE, and MR.

Experiments include multiple forecasting backbones: HiVT-64, HiVT-128, and HPNet. The HPNet transfer experiment is useful evidence that the selected subset is not purely tied to the selection backbone.

The balanced selection variant shows consistent gains over random sampling and fixed-ratio selection on dense-agent validation subsets, especially at lower keep ratios, supporting the claim that difficulty-aware allocation can improve performance on rare complex cases.
The method is simple and potentially useful in practice if clarified and validated further, since selecting real samples is easier to deploy than synthetic dataset distillation.
weaknesses: The central technical formulation is not convincing as written. Equation (1) is described as a submodular function, but it is defined as a per-sample score involving the current coreset and its complement rather than a clear set function P(C). No proof or even precise argument is provided that the objective is submodular or that greedy selection has any approximation property.

The interpretation of Eq. (1) appears internally inconsistent: squared distances are called similarities, and maximizing the first positive distance term would favor samples far from the selected set, while the text says it measures alignment with selected samples. This raises concern that the method is either misstated or conceptually confused.

The data-efficiency claim is weakened because coreset construction requires pretraining HiVT-64 on the full dataset for 10 epochs and computing scores for all samples. The paper does not report coreset construction cost, total GPU time, or whether the end-to-end pipeline is actually cheaper than standard training.

Experimental comparisons are too limited. Random sampling is the only external baseline, despite many relevant subset-selection methods cited in the paper, such as k-center/features, forgetting/entropy, gradient matching, GLISTER/GradMatch-style approaches, or submodular facility-location variants.

The evaluation is restricted to Argoverse 1.1 validation splits. There is no test-set/server evaluation, no cross-dataset experiment, and no evidence that the selected coreset generalizes beyond validation subsets derived from the same dataset.

The dense-scenario evaluation is useful but incomplete: validation subsets with more than 40/60/80 agents may be small and correlated with the selection criterion, yet sample counts, confidence intervals, and repeated trials are not reported. Random subset results appear to be single runs, so variance is unknown.

Important implementation details are missing or ambiguous, including the threshold for filtering infrequent agents, exact difficulty binning, how f(S) is computed and cached, whether labels/future trajectories are used during selection, random seeds, and how budget rounding is handled.

The balanced budget algorithm is underspecified and potentially problematic. It prioritizes high-density bins and can substantially alter the training distribution, but the paper does not analyze the tradeoff between improving rare dense cases and degrading ordinary-case performance.

The method’s novelty is moderate. Difficulty-aware stratified subset selection plus loss-based scoring is plausible, but the paper does not clearly distinguish its algorithmic contribution from straightforward stratified sampling with a pretrained-model score.

Presentation has several clarity issues, including inconsistent notation, awkward grammar, hard-to-read figure/table extraction in the manuscript, and claims such as 'state-of-the-art compression ratio' that are not substantiated by comparisons to prior compression methods.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant practical problem: reducing training cost for trajectory prediction while improving coverage of rare dense-traffic scenarios. This is useful for autonomous driving datasets where full retraining is expensive and easy scenarios dominate.

The idea of evaluating retained subsets not only on the standard validation set but also on denser subsets with more than 40, 60, and 80 agents is sensible and aligned with the motivation about safety-critical rare scenarios.
The experiments include several backbone models, including HiVT-64, HiVT-128, and HPNet, which provides some evidence that selected subsets are not completely tied to the model used for selection.

The balanced sampling results suggest a plausible benefit on dense-agent validation subsets, especially at small keep ratios, and the paper reports distribution statistics showing that the selected data are less skewed than random subsets.
weaknesses: The central technical formulation is weak and unclear. The proposed submodular function is not convincingly shown to be submodular, and the definition in Eq. 1 appears inconsistent with the accompanying explanation: squared differences are described as similarity, while maximizing them would favor dissimilarity. This undermines the technical correctness of the main method.

The paper claims novelty and a strong compression ratio, but compares primarily against random sampling and an internal fixed/balanced variant. It does not compare to relevant data selection or coreset baselines such as gradient/feature/proxy selection methods, nor to simpler stratified sampling by agent count, making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed submodular scoring.

The experimental evidence is too narrow for the claims. Evaluation is limited to Argoverse 1.1, with no cross-dataset test, no test-set submission, no runtime or training-cost accounting for the selection procedure, and no statistical variation over random seeds. Since coreset construction requires pretraining HiVT-64 for 10 epochs and scoring samples, the actual computational savings are not quantified.

The definition of scenario difficulty as only the number of agents is simplistic and insufficiently justified. Dense scenes can be easier than sparse but interactive cases, and the paper does not analyze other difficulty factors such as map topology, maneuver type, interaction risk, or prediction error under a pretrained model.

The algorithm and implementation details are underspecified. Filtering agents by frequency is not precisely defined, the dynamic budget can produce non-integer sample counts, and the pseudocode/resetting of remaining budget is ambiguous. Reproducibility would be difficult without code and more exact selection/scoring details.

Several reported results are not as strong as the framing suggests. For example, on HPNet with more than 40 agents, the 50% balanced coreset still degrades minADE/minFDE/MR relative to full-data training, and the benefits over fixed selection are modest at larger keep ratios. The paper does not fully quantify tradeoffs on the full validation set versus dense subsets.

The presentation has significant clarity issues, including awkward writing, hard-to-read figures/tables, imprecise claims such as state-of-the-art compression ratio, and missing discussion of limitations. These are not merely cosmetic because they obscure the method and weaken confidence in the evidence.

strengths: The paper tackles a useful and timely problem: reducing training data for trajectory prediction while improving coverage of rare, dense traffic scenarios. This is practically relevant because motion forecasting models are expensive to train and safety-critical cases are often underrepresented.

The main idea of combining coreset selection with difficulty-aware allocation is simple, intuitive, and well matched to the domain. Using agent count as a proxy for scenario difficulty is imperfect, but it is transparent and empirically tied to the paper's dense-traffic analysis.

The empirical results are encouraging. On Argoverse 1.1, training with 50% selected data gives performance close to full-data training for HiVT variants, and the balanced strategy improves results on high-agent-count validation subsets. For example, on the >60-agent subset, balanced selection at 40% data improves HiVT-64 minADE over random selection, and in some dense settings even outperforms the full-data model.

The paper includes some evidence of transferability: coresets selected with HiVT-64 are also evaluated on HPNet, where balanced selection retains competitive performance across multiple keep ratios. This helps support the claim that the selected data are not purely overfit to the selection backbone.

The motivation and high-level method are generally clear, and the paper presents results across several keep ratios, models, and difficulty partitions rather than only reporting one favorable compression point.
weaknesses: The technical formulation of the proposed submodular objective is not fully convincing. Equation 1 defines a score for an individual sample rather than a set function, the relationship to the stated marginal gain is unclear, and no proof or citation establishes that the objective is actually submodular. The interpretation of the two distance terms is also confusing: squared loss differences are described as similarity, while maximizing the expression appears to reward distance from selected samples and penalize distance from unselected samples.

Important implementation details are under-specified, which limits reproducibility. The filtering rule for infrequently appearing agents is not quantitatively defined, the exact construction of f(S) is unclear beyond naming the losses, rounding/tie-breaking for budgets is not specified, and the computational cost of scoring all samples is not reported.

The experimental comparison is too narrow. Random sampling is the only substantial baseline, but the paper should compare against stratified sampling by agent count, loss-based selection, herding/facility-location style coreset methods, gradient-based subset selection, or simpler oversampling/reweighting strategies for dense scenarios. Without these, it is hard to know how much of the gain comes from the proposed submodular score versus difficulty balancing alone.

The evaluation is limited to Argoverse 1.1 validation splits. There is no test-server result, no second dataset such as Argoverse 2/Waymo/nuScenes, and no analysis of robustness across random seeds. This weakens claims about generalization and state-of-the-art compression ratio.

The paper does not clearly quantify the actual efficiency tradeoff. It reports reduced training data, but not end-to-end selection time, GPU hours saved, pretraining overhead for the selection backbone, memory cost, or whether the selection process itself offsets the training savings at different keep ratios.

The notion of difficulty is reduced to the number of agents, which may miss other hard cases such as unusual maneuvers, map topology, occlusion, interaction type, or long-tail behavior. The balanced method may therefore improve dense-scene coverage without necessarily addressing broader trajectory prediction difficulty.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, including being the first effective large-scale trajectory dataset condensation method and achieving a state-of-the-art compression ratio. The manuscript does not provide a broad enough comparison to substantiate these claims.

Presentation quality is adequate but uneven. Figure 2 is dense and difficult to read, several explanations repeat high-level motivation rather than clarifying algorithmic details, and the method section would benefit from a more precise mathematical definition of the objective and selection procedure.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem for trajectory prediction: reducing training cost while mitigating poor performance on underrepresented high-density traffic scenes. This is a useful data-centric angle for autonomous driving benchmarks.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for the main claim: Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2 are both used, and the selected subsets are evaluated across several trajectory prediction models, including HiVT-64/128, HPNet, QCNet, and DeMo.

The results consistently show that SSTP outperforms random selection, k-means, and herding at matched retention ratios. For example, on Argoverse 1 at 50% retention, HiVT-64 improves from 0.750/1.175/0.137 for random selection to 0.704/1.073/0.111, close to full-data training at 0.695/1.037/0.109.

The high-density analysis is a meaningful contribution: the 50% SSTP subset improves over full-data training for scenes with at least 60 or 80 agents, suggesting that the density balancing component addresses a real dataset imbalance rather than only compressing data.

The ablations are helpful: the paper separates density partitioning from submodular/gradient-based selection and studies retention ratio, partition interval, pretraining epochs, and selection-backbone transfer.
weaknesses: The method is technically under-specified and not fully justified. The paper calls the objective a submodular gain function, but it defines a per-sample score rather than a clear set function with a stated submodularity property or approximation guarantee. This matters because the claimed optimization rationale is stronger than what is demonstrated.

The efficiency claims are only partially supported. SSTP requires pretraining a backbone on the full dataset and computing per-sample gradients, but the selection overhead and pretraining assumptions are not consistently accounted for. For HiVT, the reported total of 2.17 hours selection plus 4.20 hours subset training saves only about 1.4 hours versus 7.78 hours full training, which is less compelling than the headline framing suggests.

Reproducibility is weak in the submitted manuscript. The code link is incomplete, and important details are missing, including exact pretrained checkpoints, loss implementation for gradient extraction across different backbones, hardware/settings for all timing results, random seeds, and whether random-selection baselines are averaged over multiple draws.

The baselines are somewhat limited relative to the data-selection literature. The paper compares to random, k-means, and herding, but does not include stronger gradient/coreset methods such as GradMatch-style selection or proxy-based selection adapted to the task, making it hard to assess whether the proposed gradient-density combination is state of the art among selection methods.

Some claims overreach the evidence. The paper states model-agnostic behavior and broad applicability, but selection is mainly based on HiVT-64 or QCNet and transfer is shown on a small set of closely related trajectory models/datasets. Similarly, the conclusion claims broad robustness while evaluation remains within Argoverse-style benchmarks.

The overall full-dataset accuracy is not improved in most settings; SSTP is primarily a cost/long-tail tradeoff. This is valuable, but the paper should frame the contribution more carefully because several tables show small degradations versus full-data training on aggregate metrics.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: there are typos and grammatical problems, some table captions/claims are imprecise, and Figure/table discussions occasionally mention results not clearly shown in the main paper, such as broader Argoverse 2 high-density behavior and supplementary retention-ratio details.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing training cost for trajectory prediction while paying attention to long-tail/high-density traffic scenarios, which is relevant for autonomous driving safety.

The proposed framework is simple and potentially useful: partition scenes by agent count, compute gradient/embedding features from a pretrained predictor, and select a smaller subset with a diversity-oriented criterion.
Experiments cover two common benchmarks, Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2, and several trajectory prediction backbones, including HiVT, HPNet, QCNet, and DeMo.

The reported results consistently show SSTP outperforming random, k-means, and herding selection at matched retention ratios, and the high-density breakdown suggests meaningful gains on underrepresented crowded scenes.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is limited. The method is largely a combination of density-based rebalancing and known gradient/coreset-style sample selection, but the paper does not clearly establish what is algorithmically novel beyond applying these ideas to trajectory prediction.

The claimed submodular formulation is insufficiently justified. The paper defines a score using similarities to selected and unselected samples and greedily chooses an argmin, but it does not prove or convincingly explain submodularity, monotonicity, or any approximation property. This weakens the central methodological claim.

The method is under-specified. Important implementation details are missing, including how gradients are aggregated across agents, modes, timesteps, and decoder layers; how the latent vector is chosen; how dimensional compatibility in the elementwise gradient-latent product is ensured; and the computational/memory cost of storing pairwise similarities or gradient features.

The efficiency claim is only partially supported. SSTP requires pretraining on the full dataset for selection, and for HiVT the reported total time is 6.37 hours versus 7.78 hours, a modest saving once selection cost is included. The paper emphasizes large savings for HPNet, but this depends on reusing a subset selected by another model and does not fully analyze the one-time selection cost, hardware comparability, or amortization assumptions.

Evaluation baselines are weak for a sample-selection paper. Comparisons are limited mainly to random, k-means, and herding, while stronger and more directly relevant coreset/gradient-based selection methods such as GradMatch/CRAIG/GLISTER-style approaches are not adapted or compared.

The main average-metric results are not as strong as the prose suggests. At 50% retention, SSTP remains worse than full-data training on most overall minADE/minFDE/MR results; its clearest advantage is in high-density subsets. That is valuable, but the paper sometimes overstates this as broadly comparable or better performance.

The high-density analysis is promising but narrow. The most important safety-oriented claim relies on limited density bins and appears mainly demonstrated for selected model/dataset settings; there is no uncertainty analysis, seed variation, statistical testing, or broader rare-scenario taxonomy beyond agent count.

Some claims are internally inconsistent or imprecise. For example, the text refers to improvements on Argoverse 2 with HPNet although HPNet is not the reported Argoverse 2 evaluation model, and the abstract/code availability line contains a placeholder GitHub URL. These issues raise reproducibility and polish concerns.

Reproducibility is currently poor. The code link is incomplete, training/selection hyperparameters are sparse, random seeds and variance are absent, and the exact selected-subset construction procedure is not detailed enough to confidently reproduce the results.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and practical problem: reducing the training cost of modern trajectory prediction models while improving behavior on underrepresented high-density scenes. This is useful for autonomous driving research where full-dataset training can be expensive.

The proposed SSTP framework is simple and well motivated: partition scenarios by agent density, extract gradient/embedding features from a lightly pretrained predictor, and greedily select representative samples with a similarity-based criterion. The method is easy to understand and plausibly transferable across model architectures.

Empirical support is fairly broad for a CVPR submission: experiments cover Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2, multiple predictors (HiVT-64/128, HPNet, QCNet, DeMo), several retention ratios, and comparisons against random, k-means, and herding selection. SSTP consistently outperforms these subset baselines and approaches full-data performance with 40-60% of the data.

The high-density analysis is a strong point. Table 4 shows that the 50% SSTP subset improves over full-data training in the rare high-agent regimes while only modestly degrading low-density performance, which supports the paper's central claim about mitigating imbalance rather than merely compressing data.

The ablations are meaningful: separating partitioning and submodular selection shows that both density balancing and informativeness contribute, while experiments on pretraining epochs, backbone choice, and partition interval provide useful robustness evidence.

The efficiency argument is practically appealing: the authors account for selection time for HiVT and still show a net reduction, and the selected subset can be reused to train other models, making the approach potentially valuable even when it does not beat full-dataset aggregate metrics.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. The core ingredients are stratified sampling by scene density plus gradient/feature-based coreset-style selection with a greedy similarity criterion. The paper would be stronger if it positioned itself more carefully against broader data pruning/coreset methods beyond random, k-means, and herding, especially gradient-based sample selection methods from general deep learning.

The technical formulation of the claimed submodular objective is not fully rigorous. The paper defines a per-sample score P(S_j) depending on the current selected set, but does not clearly define a set function, prove submodularity, or justify the greedy approximation guarantee. The sign and interpretation of the objective also deserve more explanation, since the argmin of the stated difference of similarities is not immediately transparent.

The efficiency accounting is incomplete and somewhat inconsistent. Selection requires pretraining on the full dataset for several epochs and computing gradients/features for all samples; the runtime, memory cost, and scaling behavior of this stage are not analyzed in enough detail. Reported HPNet training times also vary across Table 1, Figure 1, and Section 4.4, which weakens confidence in the exact savings.

The comparison set is narrower than ideal. There is no comparison to recent long-tail trajectory methods, active learning/data pruning criteria, uncertainty or loss-based selection, or simpler density-stratified random sampling with matched distribution. This makes it hard to know how much of the gain comes from the proposed gradient-submodular criterion versus density rebalancing plus a strong but simple heuristic.

Reproducibility has notable gaps. The manuscript contains a placeholder code URL, lacks some implementation details for selection such as default interval choices, feature normalization, batching, recomputation strategy, and selection hyperparameters, and does not report variance across random seeds or repeated subset selection runs.

The aggregate full-dataset performance remains slightly better than SSTP in many standard metrics, so the acceptance case depends on the efficiency and high-density improvements. That tradeoff is reasonable, but the paper should be careful not to overstate 'comparable or better' performance without specifying that the main gains are in rare dense scenarios and training cost.

Presentation has several polish issues, including grammar errors, awkward phrasing, table formatting problems, and a placeholder repository link. These do not undermine the contribution but do affect clarity and reproducibility.
